## Five Number Summaries

A common method of looking at quantitative data is with a boxplot. There are 6 components that make up the boxplot.

- **Minimum** - the smallest value

- **Lower quartile (Q1)** - value for which 25% of the data lie below ("median" of minimum and median

- **Median** - the middle value (if there is an even number of values, then take the average of the two values in the middle)

- **Upper Quartile (Q3)** - the value for which 75% of the data lie below ("median" of median and max)

- **Maximum** - the largest value

- **Outliers** - unusual extreme values in the data

![](media/image2.png)

**Interquartile range**

- ![](media/image3.png)![](media/image4.png)The difference between \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

- This will be resistant to outliers

**Boxplot**

- Visual display of the five number summary

## Boxplot Example

Suppose you collected the following ten values from your sample:

![](media/image5.png)23 22 27 23 28 26 27 27 25 21

The first step is to arrange the numbers in order from least to greatest:

![](media/image6.png)![](media/image7.png)21 22 23 23 25 26 27 27 27 28

![](media/image8.png)![](media/image9.png)

Since there is an even count of values, we need to take the average of the two values in the middle. Here, the values are 25 and 26, so the median is 25.5.

![](media/image10.png)![](media/image11.png)**Note:** There appears to be a discrepancy in the calculations of Q1 and Q3. I have seen some software include the use of the median and other software exclude the median. However, this discrepancy is negligible because the goal of quartiles for summarizing data is to get an idea of how the data behaves. In this class, you are not expected to calculate quartiles other than the median.

![](media/image12.png)![](media/image13.png)![](media/image14.png)

![](media/image15.png)![](media/image16.png)![](media/image17.png)Boxplot on the data

![](media/image18.png)![](media/image19.png)21 22 23 23 25 26 27 27 27 28

Boxplot to scale

![](media/image20.png)![](media/image21.png)![Chart, box and whisker chart Description automatically generated](media/image22.png){width="2.7777777777777777in" height="4.166666666666667in"}

Here, you can see that Q1 is 23 and Q3 is 27. Therefore, the interquartile range is $27 - 23 = 4$

To find outliers, check values that are $Q1 - 1.5 \cdot IQR$ or $Q3 + 1.5 \cdot IQR$. Some software programs use points on the plot to specify values that are outliers.

## Notation

![](media/image43.png)

+---------------+-------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
|               | **Categorical**                           | **Quantitative**                                           |
|               |                                           |                                                            |
|               | **(2 Groups)**                            | ![](media/image44.png)![](media/image45.png)**(2 Groups)** |
+:=============:+:=========================================:+:==========================================================:+
| Parameter     | $$\pi_{1} - \pi_{2}$$                     | $$\mu_{1} - \mu_{2}$$                                      |
+---------------+-------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Statistic     | $${\widehat{p}}_{1} - {\widehat{p}}_{2}$$ | $${\overline{x}}_{1} - {\overline{x}}_{2}$$                |
+---------------+-------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+

**Parameter:** The long run difference in average "context" between "group 1" and "group 2"

**Important note:** This is not the same as "The long run average difference." We will talk more about this in Chapter 7.

# Section 6.3

## Parameters and Hypotheses

**Parameter:**

Long run difference in average "context here" between group 1 and group 2

**Hypotheses:**

Symbols

$$H_{0}:\ \mu_{Group\ 1}\  - \ \mu_{Group\ 2} = 0$$

$$H_{A}:\ \mu_{Group\ 1}\  - \ \mu_{Group\ 2} > OR < OR \neq 0$$

**Words**

Null: The long run difference in average "context" between group 1 and group 2 is equal to zero

Alt: The long run difference in average "context" between group 1 and group 2 \_\_\_\_\_\_ zero

## Validity conditions

1)  At least 20 observations in each group

2)  Distributions are not strongly skewed

## Standard Error

The standard error for two means is as follows:

$$SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}$$

## Two Sample T-test (Standardized Statistic)

$$t = \frac{\left( {\overline{x}}_{Group\ 1}\  - \ {\overline{x}}_{Group\ 2} \right) - 0\ }{SE} = \frac{{\overline{x}}_{\ 1}\  - \ {\overline{x}}_{\ 2}}{\sqrt{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}}$$

## Confidence Interval

![](media/image46.png)

$${\overline{x}}_{\ 1}\  - \ {\overline{x}}_{\ 2} \pm multipler\ *\sqrt{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}$$

Formal Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the long run difference in average **"*context"*** between "***group A"*** and **"*group B"*** falls between \_\_\_\_\_\_ and \_\_\_\_\_\_.

## Example (Bike; in class)

A bike company wants to test the effect of two brands of bike tires (Roadster and Trail-days) on the amount of miles ridden before the tires wear out. The company randomly selects 40 customers from their records and ask them to participate in the study in exchange for free tires. The participants were randomly assigned to either tire (20 participants to each tire brand). The data is summarized below, and you may assume that the data was not strongly skewed. Did the Roaster bike tires on average get more miles than the Trail-days tires?
